title: The widow of Nain (Luke 7:11–17)
hook: he sees a widow burying her only son and says: don't weep

segments.voice: Yesterday: a centurion who said I am not worthy, and your line, only say the word.

Two crowds on one road. One is coming toward a small town called Nain: Jesus, his disciples, and a lot of people following, talking, full of the news from Capernaum. The other is coming out of the town gate. Slow. Quiet, except for the crying. A funeral. Men carry a body on an open bier, and behind them walks a woman. Luke says it in one sentence: the dead man was "the only son of his mother, and she was a widow." She has already buried her husband. Now her only son. And the two crowds meet at the gate.
screen: `AN ONLY SON, AND SHE A WIDOW.`

segments.voice: Some readers point out that in that world a widow with no son could be left without income or protection. If so, she is burying her child and her future on the same day. Then Luke writes: "And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not." Nobody asks him for anything. No one sends for him, no friends lower anyone through a roof. He sees her, and that's enough. The Greek for compassion is splanchnizomai, related to a word for the inner organs; some translate it as being moved in the gut, a pull deep inside at someone else's pain. Then something unexpected at a funeral: "he came and touched the bier: and they that bare him stood still." The whole procession stops. "And he said, Young man, I say unto thee, Arise. And he that was dead sat up, and began to speak. And he delivered him to his mother." That last phrase nearly repeats the words of 1 Kings about Elijah, when he raised a widow's son in Zarephath. The crowd says, "a great prophet is risen up among us," and, "God hath visited his people." This story begins not with a request or with faith, but with noticing a grieving stranger and being moved. Christian readers have seen God's own heart there: a God who sees the widow before anyone asks.
screen: then, large: `WHEN THE LORD SAW HER, HE HAD COMPASSION ON HER.`

segments.voice: Grief is often quiet: the man sitting too long in his parked car, the woman on the train staring at nothing, a voice on the phone worn thin. Bring to mind a stranger who might have been carrying something, and without needing their story, breathe in their heaviness and breathe out care toward them. If you pray, you can hold that stranger before God; if you don't, simply wish them well.
Splanchnizomai, Luke's Greek word for being moved with compassion, deep in the gut: a mother burying her only son meets Jesus at the gate, and before anyone asks, he is moved and gives her son back.
Your line: he had compassion on her. Nobody had to ask; he saw her, and that was enough. Day five hundred twenty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Some churches read the widow of Nain at funerals and in times of grief, as a picture of Jesus noticing sorrow before anyone asks.

chat.meaning: Luke says when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her. Nobody asked; he saw her, and that was enough.

bier.meaning: an open frame for carrying the dead

Zarephath.meaning: the town where Elijah raised a widow's son

notes: The widow's economic vulnerability is a standard historical reading. Confirm framing.
splanchnizomai from splanchna (inner organs): standard lexicon.
Echo of 1 Kings 17:23 ('delivered him unto his mother') is widely noted, and the Greek (Septuagint and Luke) match closely. Confirm 'almost word for word'.
